nameStory: Snow-in-summer gets its charming name from the way its masses of small white flowers blanket the silvery foliage, creating the illusion of fresh snow covering the ground during the warm summer months. The contrast between the pure white blooms and the felty gray-green leaves makes this Mediterranean native look like winter has arrived in your garden, even on the hottest July day.
description: Snow-in-summer is a low-growing, spreading perennial that forms dense mats of silvery-gray foliage topped with clusters of bright white, star-shaped flowers. This hardy ground cover typically stays under 6 inches tall but can spread widely, making it popular in rock gardens and as a border plant. Originally from the alpine regions of Italy, it's now commonly grown as an ornamental throughout New England, though it occasionally escapes cultivation.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, narrow leaves covered in dense, soft white hairs that give them a distinctive felty or woolly texture - run your fingers over them and they feel like velvet

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Pure white, star-shaped flowers about half an inch across with five deeply notched petals that give each bloom a distinctive raggedy appearance

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats that hug the ground, with stems that root as they spread outward from the center

idTips.label: Overall Color
idTips.description: Distinctive silvery-gray appearance year-round due to the dense white hairs covering all the foliage, making it stand out even when not blooming

habitat: In New England, snow-in-summer is most commonly found in cultivated settings like rock gardens, borders, and as ground cover in sunny, well-drained areas. It occasionally escapes to disturbed sites, roadsides, and areas near homes where it can establish in poor, rocky soils. This Mediterranean native thrives in full sun and tolerates drought once established.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as silvery-gray mats expand, with the characteristic felty leaves becoming more prominent as temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time, when masses of white star-shaped flowers create the 'snow' effect that gives this plant its name, typically from late May through July.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade but the distinctive silvery foliage remains prominent and continues to spread, maintaining its ornamental value.
seasonality.winter: In milder winters, the woolly gray foliage may persist, though it often dies back partially, leaving the spreading root system to regenerate in spring.

funFact: The dense white hairs covering snow-in-summer's leaves aren't just for show - they're actually a survival adaptation from its alpine origins that reflects intense sunlight and reduces water loss, essentially giving the plant its own built-in sunscreen and moisturizer!
confusionNotes: Snow-in-summer's felty, silvery leaves make it nearly unmistakable among the chickweeds - other mouse-ear chickweeds have much greener, less hairy foliage. Memory trick: if it looks like it's covered in gray felt, it's snow-in-summer; if it's just regular green and slightly fuzzy, it's one of the other chickweeds.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name suggesting it's a summer-blooming native, snow-in-summer is actually a European alpine plant that has become popular in American gardens. Don't let the name fool you into thinking it's related to other 'summer' plants - it's firmly in the chickweed family.
compareHints: Snow-in-summer stands out dramatically from its mouse-ear chickweed relatives due to its distinctive 'tomentose' or felty white hairs covering the entire plant, giving it a silvery appearance. While other chickweeds in the genus may have some fuzzy hairs, none have the dense, woolly coating that makes snow-in-summer look like it's perpetually dusted with powder. Most other Cerastium species are also much greener and less ornamental in appearance.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its mouse-ear chickweed relatives, common mouse-ear chickweed is the most widespread and persistent in New England.
Field chickweed stands out from its mouse-ear relatives by forming the densest, most mat-like growth habit and having the most deeply notched flower petals.
Among the mouse-ear chickweeds in New England, sticky mouse-ear is the only one with that distinctive clammy, tacky feel from its glandular hairs.
American field chickweed differs from other Cerastium species by having the most deeply divided petals - they're split nearly to the base.
Among the mouse-ear chickweeds in New England, common mouse-ear chickweed is the most widespread and has the most consistently fuzzy texture throughout the plant.
Little mouse-ear is smaller and more delicate than common mouse-ear chickweed, which is perennial and has longer petals.
Unlike the very common mouse-ear chickweed which has fuzzy, spoon-shaped leaves and upright flowers, nodding chickweed has narrower leaves and distinctively drooping flowers.
Among its mouse-ear relatives, dwarf mouse-ear stands out for being the tiniest and having petals that don't extend beyond the sepals.
